doc.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

chapter: Jump Town and the Ventura band
title: Voices an octave apart and the counterpoint of 'Cheerful Little Earful'
summary: How their voices a perfect octave apart work with horns, unison, harmony and counterpoint, using last night's performance as example.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: At that point did you have an idea of how the voicing worked best with the voice amidst the horns?

Well the thing is, our voices are an octave apart. A perfect octave. We have the same range top to bottom, which makes it easier. You don’t have to jump octaves to sing the same song or anything. Now with the horn all we have to do is I have to write the horn in to what we’re doing, period.

And a lot of things we did were actually unison but because of the chords that were used and because of our voices being an octave apart, it sounded really like we were almost doing harmony some of the time.
When two instruments play perfect octaves, then in between are all these overtones. And so the two voices, when we sing in tune — once in a while—

And also we did go into harmony too you know. I mean there were sections where we’d go into harmony and some places we did use harmony, and we did counterpuntal stuff too eventually as we went on. We kept experimenting with different things.
You heard us do “Cheerful Little Earful” last night.

Now that is — the whole thing is all two lines going counterpuntal, until we get to the ending. And you notice that I didn’t use piano until the very end. And what surprised me, and I enjoyed very much, was that after going through all this with just first drums and then the bass, and then just the bass and the drums and the two voices, when the piano finally comes in, the audience went yeahhhh. I said why do they applaud? I think it’s because they say gee they’re still in the same key.
And also I think too the fact that we sing the vocalese for two choruses and then when you finally come in with the lyrics, they think wow, that was something you know.
Oh yeah. And it built so nice, and when the piano finally comes in, it makes everything that came before it so much better, it really does.
It was a delightful, joyful experience. It just made my evening. You know — yeah.
